parts.title: Renting a musical instrument
parts.context: A mother phones a music shop to rent a violin for her son.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a music shop to rent a violin for her son. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: Melody Music Shop, Eddie speaking.

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: Hello. I'd like to rent a violin for my son, please. He's just started lessons at school.

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: Of course. We do a lot of rentals for schools. I'll take a few details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants to rent a violin, so 'violin' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: Rebecca Fitzgerald. That's F-I-T-Z-G-E-R-A-L-D.

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: Thank you, Mrs Fitzgerald. And how old is your son?

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: He's nine.

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: Violins come in different sizes, and the right one depends on the length of the child's arm, not on his age. Do you know what size he needs?

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: He's small for his age, so his teacher measured him, and she said a half size.

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: Half size, then. That's the one we'd normally give to a seven-year-old, so he'll grow out of it quickly. How long would you like to rent it for?

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: The school term is three months, but I'm not sure that he'll continue after that.

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: Three months is fine, and we can extend it if he wants to carry on. The cost is twelve pounds a month.

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: That seems reasonable.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: We also take a deposit. It's normally sixty pounds, but for school children, it's forty. You get all of it back when you return the violin undamaged.

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: That's fair. What does the rental include?

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: A bow and a case, so you don't need to buy anything else, except perhaps some rosin for the bow, which costs a couple of pounds.

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: Does he get any lessons with it?

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: We include one free trial lesson with our teacher, if you'd like it. It's a good way to check that the violin suits him.

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: Excellent. When can I collect it?

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: It will be ready on Saturday morning, after ten o'clock.

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: And what do I need to bring?

script.speaker: eddie
script.text: Some identification, please, either a passport or a driving licence, because we need to check your name and address.

script.speaker: rebecca
script.text: I'll bring my driving licence. Thanks for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A bird sanctuary
parts.context: The warden of a bird sanctuary tells visitors where to see birds.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the warden of a bird sanctuary welcoming a group of visitors. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Marsh Lake Bird Sanctuary. I'm Colin Hargreaves, the warden. Please look at the map. We're at the visitor centre, in the south, and a path goes right round the lake. It's about three kilometres, and you can walk it in an hour.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: In the south-west, close to the visitor centre, are the toilets, so please use them before you set off. There are none further round the path.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: If you go round clockwise, in the north-west, in the middle of the reeds, you'll find the reedbed hide. It's small, but it's the best place to see the shy birds that live in the reeds.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: On the north shore of the lake is the lake hide, which is the largest, with seats for thirty people, and big windows facing the water. From the north-east corner, you can see the feeding station, where we put out seed every morning, and it's always busy.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: On the east side of the lake, there's a picnic area, with tables and a good view. The building on the west side is the education hut, which we use for school groups, and the one in the south-east is the ringing hut, where we weigh and measure birds. That one is closed to the public.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: The bird we're best known for is the bittern. It's very shy and well camouflaged, so you'll hear it more often than you see it. Avocets nest on the islands in spring, and ospreys only visit us briefly on migration, so don't expect to see those.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: The best time to see birds is early in the morning, soon after we open, when they are most active. By midday, many have gone to rest, and in the evening it is usually quiet.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: When you're in the hides, please stay inside and keep still. If you go out onto the bank, the birds will be frightened by your movement and fly away, which ruins the experience for everyone.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: If you don't have binoculars, you can borrow a pair from the visitor centre. We ask for a ten-pound deposit, which we return when you bring them back.

script.speaker: hargreaves
script.text: Finally, a new project. This autumn, we're planting ten thousand reeds, to extend the reedbed, which will give the bitterns more room to breed. If you'd like to help, ask at the visitor centre. Enjoy your walk.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Reflecting on teaching practice
parts.context: Two education students compare their experiences of teaching practice.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two education students, Chloe and Daniel, discussing their teaching practice in schools. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: Daniel, how was your teaching practice? Mine ended on Friday, and I'm still exhausted.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Mine went well. What was the hardest part for you?

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: Two things. At first I couldn't keep the class quiet. They were eight years old, and they tested me all the time. And the marking. I took home thirty exercise books every night.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Was planning a problem?

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: No, the lesson plans were fine, and the school had interactive whiteboards, which made things easy. I didn't meet any parents, so that didn't come up.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: I had the opposite problem. My class was older, eleven-year-olds, so they were calmer, but I found it harder to interest them.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: Did you teach your own subject?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Mostly science, but they also asked me to run a drama club, which I loved.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: What was your most successful lesson?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: A lesson on floating and sinking. The children designed boats from foil, and tested how many coins they could carry.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: I'm sure you had a good lesson too.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: Not at first. My poetry lesson was a disaster. They were bored, so halfway through I changed the activity, and let them perform the poems instead. That worked much better.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: What did your mentor say?

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: That I was nervous about silence. She told me that a pause isn't a failure, because it gives children time to think.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: My mentor said I talk too much, and I should let the children do more of the work.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: That's good advice. Are you going to apply for jobs in this area?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: I'd like to, but there are very few posts in science. I'm also looking at schools abroad.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: I've been offered an interview already, next Wednesday.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Congratulations! I hope it goes well.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the waggle dance of honeybees
parts.context: A biology lecture on how honeybees communicate where food is.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the waggle dance of honeybees. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I'd like to talk about one of the most remarkable discoveries in animal behaviour: the way that honeybees tell each other where to find food.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The discovery was made by Karl von Frisch, an Austrian scientist, who spent decades watching bees in glass-sided hives. He shared the Nobel Prize in nineteen seventy-three for his work.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: When a forager bee finds a good source of nectar, she returns to the hive and performs a dance. The dance takes place on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, in the dark inside of the hive, and the other bees follow her, touching her with their antennae.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: If the food is close to the hive, she performs what is called a round dance. But if it is far away, she performs the waggle dance. She walks forward in a straight line while waggling her body, then circles back to the start and repeats it.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The waggle run is the key. The angle of this run, relative to the vertical, shows the direction of the food relative to the sun. If the bee waggles straight upward, the food is in the direction of the sun. If she waggles at an angle of sixty degrees to the right, the food is sixty degrees to the right of the sun.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The length of the waggle shows the distance. The longer the waggle, the further away the food. And the better the food, the more vigorous the dance, which attracts more followers.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Bees even correct for the movement of the sun across the sky, so that the information remains accurate during the day, even when the bee is inside the hive and cannot see the sun.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The same system is used in another way. When a swarm of bees looks for a new home, scouts visit possible sites, and return to dance for the sites they like. The scouts' dances compete, and the site with the most dancers is chosen. It is a remarkable example of group decision-making. Next week we'll look at ants.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
